what_it_does: Inside a chip, flip-flops are tiny circuits that store a single bit of state and capture it on each clock tick; they consume a lot of power and area. Chip designers sometimes merge several single-bit flip-flops into a single multi-bit flip-flop (MBFF) — a combined circuit that stores multiple bits at once — to save power and reduce the chip's footprint. The challenge is choosing which flip-flops to cluster: pulling them together and then adjusting their physical positions to fit the merged cell can shift them far from their original locations, which introduces delays and can degrade the chip's timing — especially when some cells are pre-placed and cannot move. This late-breaking results paper describes a method that models placement forces to nudge flip-flops toward positions that reduce displacement after merging, jointly optimizes clustering and placement legalization (the step that ensures no two cells overlap), and uses a multi-objective scoring function that balances timing, power, area, and how evenly the chip's area is used.
